name: DIY chin filler

lead: DIY chin filler is the practice of buying hyaluronic acid (HA) filler and injecting it into one's own chin, or a friend's, instead of visiting a clinic. Forum users describe it as a way to mimic bone projection, soften a recessed chin and improve the profile at a fraction of clinic cost until or instead of surgery.

The appearance payoff people report is a more forward, defined chin and a balanced profile that lasts for months as the filler is gradually absorbed. Posts show before-and-after photos and swelling updates. Professional chin filler in clinics is an established cosmetic treatment, but studies of self-injection do not exist.

paras: Forum threads describe sourcing filler online, marking the chin, using numbing cream and placing small amounts at planned points, then molding the result by hand and monitoring afterward. Posters often credit other members' guides and video threads. This wiki does not reproduce injection methods.

Regulators and surgeons warn that filler placed into a blood vessel can block it, causing skin necrosis and, in rarer cases around the face, vision loss. Infection, lumps, migration, allergic reactions and asymmetry are also reported. In many countries fillers are medical devices intended for licensed practitioners, and gray-market products may be unregulated or counterfeit.

angle.text: Chin filler adds volume to a recessed chin so the profile reads as more projected. Forum users value the low cost and reversibility compared with an implant or genioplasty. Results are temporary because HA is gradually absorbed.

lead: DIY chin filler refers to people injecting dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid, into their own chin to build projection without going to a clinician. On looksmaxxing forums it appears alongside jaw and cheek filler as a low-cost 'softmax', a non-surgical route to a stronger profile.[1][2]

Posters describe the appeal as price and control: one member says three syringes cost about 110 in total, and several describe it as a temporary stand-in until they can afford surgery.[2] Others say they are unsure whether to self-inject or visit a professional and worry about fixing mistakes.[1]

Hyaluronic acid fillers are widely used in clinics for facial contouring, and dermal filler complications, including embolic events, are described in the medical literature.[3] No published study has examined self-injection.

paras: Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring substance and the most common filler material, and most commercial HA fillers are cross-linked to resist breakdown.[3] Clinics use them for lips, cheeks and jawline, and chin augmentation is an established use.[3]

In DIY threads, users describe marking points on the chin, using topical numbing cream, injecting small amounts and shaping the result by hand. Several members post before-and-after photos, swelling-stage updates and videos.[1][4][5][6][7] This wiki does not reproduce these methods.

Members describe filler as high return for the money and as a temporary substitute for bone work while saving for surgery.[2] Other users ask whether DIY is wise compared with professional treatment and request links to earlier guides.[1][8] Experienced posters offer advice and sometimes inject friends.[1][2] Threads also feature jaw and zygomatic filler.[1]

No studies found. Studies of professionally administered filler exist, and an overview of dermal fillers notes that common effects include bruising, redness and pain, with infection, allergic reaction and lumps less common.[3]

Embolic complications are described: retrograde embolisation into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries can cause blindness, and delayed skin necrosis can occur; vision loss is usually permanent when it happens.[3]

In the US the FDA approves fillers as medical devices and a provider prescribes and performs the injection; in the UK and EEA fillers are non-prescription devices, and who may inject varies by country.[3]
